title: Paleontologist Kenneth Lacovara: Dinosaurs Were "Functionally Extinct" the Day the Asteroid Hit
excerpt: Paleontologist Kenneth Lacovara argues the strongest answer to online "dinosaurs never existed" claims isn't a debate — it's a shovel. In a…
content:
Paleontologist Kenneth Lacovara argues the strongest answer to online "dinosaurs never existed" claims isn't a debate — it's a shovel. In a wide-ranging conversation, he lays out why the fossil record is rare yet overwhelming, how deep time compresses the entire dinosaur age into roughly two weeks of a one-year Earth calendar, and why the asteroid that struck off the Yucatán wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs within about an hour of surface exposure. The impactor, up to 18 km across, blasted a crater about 110 miles wide and initially 12 miles deep; anything above ground without line-of-sight shelter was "literally toast," while burrowing mammals, crocodiles, and turtles survived. Lacovara also traces how geology itself was assembled against near-universal young-Earth belief — Isaac Newton thought the planet was 6,000 years old — and why plate tectonics took until the 1960s to win acceptance. He draws a sharp ethical line on de-extinction (mammoths yes, Neanderthals no), explains why cryptids fail the breeding-population test, and names Antarctica as paleontology's biggest open frontier. For investors, the episode is a case study in how scientific consensus forms slowly and then flips fast — a pattern that rhymes with today's debates over AI, biotechnology, and which "impossible" claims deserve capital.

Kenneth Lacovara has a simple answer for anyone who thinks dinosaurs are a hoax: go dig one up yourself. The paleontologist, who directs the Edelman Fossil Park and Museum in New Jersey, noted on The Joe Rogan Experience that the evidence isn't hidden in a vault — it's in the ground, and the museum lets the public dig above the research layer, where, he says, "every kid, every grown-up" who tries finds a 66-million-year-old fossil to take home.

That accessibility is his core rebuttal to the "dinosaurs never existed" claims circulating online. A conspiracy spanning the fossil record would have to involve continents, countries, and people who never met or lived at the same time. As Rogan put it, the fossil record is hard to fake at scale. But the deeper story Lacovara tells over the conversation isn't about denialism at all — it's about how a handful of 17th- and 18th-century thinkers figured out that the planet is billions of years old, and why that single idea made everything else, from evolution to plate tectonics, possible.

Fossilization is nearly impossible — which is why the record is trustworthy

The chance that any individual organism becomes a fossil is close to zero. But the experiment runs across hundreds of millions of years and countless individuals. Lacovara endorses the framing that "unlikely things are likely to happen when happening happens a lot."

The mechanism matters, and it's where a lot of public misunderstanding sits. Fossilization has to begin fast, or the body decays or weathers away. An organism trapped in mineral-rich mud can reach "subfossil" status in months to years, he says, while full mineralization into rock can take thousands of years or longer. Permineralization works like the scale on a shower head — groundwater carries dissolved minerals that precipitate into the bone's pore spaces, leaving a mineral copy of the original. The La Brea tar pits, famous for saber-toothed cats, hold subfossils rather than true fossils, because the original bone material is largely still there.

ClaimLacovara's position
Dinosaur fossils are fakes or recreationsRecreations exist and are labeled, but real bones underpin them; the conspiracy would be unscaleable
Fossilization takes millions of yearsInitial stabilization happens in months to years; full lithification can take far longer
Complete skeletons don't exist"Nearly complete" specimens like Leonardo the Brachylophosaurus are effectively complete; completeness is a spectrum
Blood and soft tissue in dinosaur bonePossible; he cites Mary Schweitzer's caution that the reported blood cells lack the nuclear bulge expected and were bulk-sampled, so the jury is still out

He's also candid about what the record can't tell us. Fossils are biased toward lowland environments — flood plains and coastlines where sediment accumulates. Dinosaurs that lived in mountains, which shed sediment rather than trap it, would almost never fossilize. "Nearly all" dinosaur species that ever lived are unknown to science, he says, and the biggest individual of any species is unlikely ever to be found. The record is a sample, not a census — and it's still overwhelming.

Deep time squeezes the dinosaur age into two weeks of a single year

Lacovara's most quotable device is a calendar. Compress Earth's 4.567 billion years into one year, and complex life — trilobites and their kin — doesn't show up until around Thanksgiving, roughly half a billion years ago. The first dinosaurs appear in the second week of December. They persist for about 165 million years, until the asteroid strikes "the day after Christmas." And our own species? "Homo sapiens shows up 300,000 years ago," he says. "That's about 20 seconds before midnight on the last night of the year."

The point isn't trivia. It's that dinosaurs are recent neighbors, not ancient abstractions — "only 2% of Earth history ago," as he puts it. That recency is why so many skeletons survive to be found at all.

The impact itself is where the calendar analogy turns visceral. Lacovara dates it to about 66 million years ago: an asteroid up to 18 km across striking off the Yucatán, excavating a crater roughly 110 miles wide and initially about 12 miles deep. To convey that depth, he compares it to the Grand Canyon, which is about one mile deep. The pulverized rock — a volume he sizes at Massachusetts times 12 miles — was thrown into the atmosphere, gaining gravitational potential energy that came back as friction. Within an hour, surface temperatures hit "somewhere between toaster oven and pizza oven." Anything on the surface was, in his words, "literally toast."

Survival came down to whether you could get underground. The heat was radiative, not convective — "like those outdoor restaurant heaters," he says. "It's line of sight. So you got to get out of the line of sight of the sky." Every non-avian dinosaur egg nest ever found sits on the surface, meaning 100% of their life cycle was exposed. Small mammals, crocodiles, turtles, lizards, and some burrowing birds got through. "I think they're functionally extinct the day of the impact," Lacovara says. "They're around for 65 million years, right? Dominating the Earth for most of that time." Sixty-five million years of dominance, erased in an afternoon.

Geology was built against near-universal young-Earth belief

What makes the modern view remarkable isn't just that it's correct — it's how recently it was assembled. Lacovara traces the thread to Nicolaus Steno in the 1600s, who argued that "serpent tongues" found in Sicilian fields were actually shark teeth, and who formulated three laws of geology still in use: oldest rock on the bottom, youngest on top; matching rock on both sides of a valley was once connected; and strata record sequence.

James Hutton, publishing Theory of the Earth around 1795 while dying, used Siccar Point in Scotland — tilted, cross-cut, lithified beach sediments later uplifted into a coastline — to argue the planet was ancient. His principle of uniformitarianism, that "the present is the key to the past," was popularized by Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology. The context Lacovara stresses: Isaac Newton thought Earth was 6,000 years old. Darwin boarded the Beagle a young-Earth creationist. Captain Fitzroy handed him Lyell's first volume; Darwin held the expedition at Montevideo waiting for the second. By Patagonia, he was paraphrasing Lyell. That intellectual space — deep time — is what let Darwin imagine natural selection at all. He then sat on the idea for 25 years before publishing Origin of Species, taking nine years off to become the world's expert on barnacles.

Plate tectonics is even more recent. Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in the 1920s and was dismissed for lacking a mechanism. Harry Hess, a US Navy officer and Princeton professor, developed magnetometers for submarine detection during World War II, noticed ocean-floor magnetic striping parallel to mid-ocean ridges, and proposed seafloor spreading — new crust created at ridges, with magnetic polarity recorded as Earth's field flips. Lacovara notes he studied under professors who were "pre-plate tectonics," still shoehorning the older geosynclinal theory into the new framework. He cites Max Planck's line that science advances "one funeral at a time."

The magnetic field flips on an irregular schedule, and nobody knows exactly what happens next

Earth's magnetosphere exists because a solid iron-nickel inner core rotates at a different speed from the liquid outer core — "metal rotating inside metal," effectively a generator. Reversals average roughly every 800,000 years, with the last about 800,000 years ago, but the interval is highly variable. Lacovara notes a roughly 5-million-year span at the end of the Cretaceous with no flip, which removes a key correlation tool for rocks of that age — the exact interval where he works.

On consequences, he's candid that this is outside his field and not well established. His guess: increased cancer and mutation rates, possibly acting as an evolutionary spur, but "I can't imagine anybody would think of it as a good thing." Rogan reads a Perplexity answer stating that reversals weaken but do not eliminate the field, that the atmosphere remains a substantial shield, and that evidence does not support mass extinction. The tool also surfaces the disputed 2021 "Adams event" hypothesis — a temporary reversal about 42,000 years ago proposed as contributing to Australian megafauna and Neanderthal decline. Lacovara flags it as disputed rather than established, and notes magnetic navigation in birds and marine animals would be disrupted.

Cryptids fail one simple test, but real "impossible" animals keep turning up

Lacovara's skepticism about lake monsters and ape-men is structural, not snobbish: a breeding population is required, and "you're not going to miss a thousand plesiosaur-like creatures in Loch Ness." The Mokele-mbembe — a Congo creature described by locals as a long-necked, reddish-brown animal with a rooster-like frill, the size of an elephant or hippo — has drawn expeditions including microbiologist Roy Mackal's in the 1980s, with no physical evidence. Rogan notes the description sounds feathered, and that the Congo is vast, dangerous, and hard to fund.

Against that, the episode stacks real discoveries that once sounded like cryptids: the okapi, unknown to science until the last century; the "Bili ape," a population of unusually large ground-nesting chimpanzees in the Congo documented by photographer Karl Ammann from the 1990s, with camera-trap photos, fecal samples, and bones, and individuals reportedly up to six feet tall; and Homo floresiensis, the "hobbit" of Flores, initially dismissed as a pathological individual and now accepted as a species. Lacovara notes the hominin family tree is a bush — it's unusual for only one human species to be alive.

He also explains folk paleontology, drawing on Adrienne Mayor's work: ancient people found fossils and made explanations. Protoceratops — beaked, quadrupedal — may underlie the griffin. Dwarf elephant skulls on Mediterranean islands, with their single coalesced nasal opening, may underlie the cyclops. Steno's shark teeth became "serpent tongues." The through-line is that people explain their landscape with the framework they have — which is, in a sense, what the dinosaur deniers are doing too.

De-extinction ethics split sharply between animals and humans

Lacovara is an adviser to Colossal Biosciences and calls visiting "like being in a movie." He draws a line: mammoths (the last ones on Wrangel Island died about 3,000 years ago, in a world of pyramids and beer), thylacines, dodos, and bluebucks went extinct largely by human hand, and "their ecosystem is still here." He offers a thought experiment: if the cheetah went extinct Monday, would you bring it back Tuesday? A year later? A thousand years later, when the ecosystem has adjusted? He notes the pronghorn's speed is an adaptation to cheetahs that no longer exist in North America.

On Neanderthals and Denisovans, he is firmly opposed. He cites Beth Shapiro's point that Neanderthal genes scattered across living humans could collectively reconstruct nearly the entire Neanderthal genome — "wildly unethical." Rogan presses the inconsistency: society accepts mammoth de-extinction with little pushback but would recoil at a Neanderthal. Lacovara agrees the asymmetry is real and says nobody he knows wants to attempt it. On zoo ethics, he recounts an elephant at the National Zoo scraping a rock against the sidewalk and then its own leg, comparing hardness — evidence of a thinking being. He says primate cages in particular bother him, while crediting zoos' conservation role, including the California condor recovery from about 22 individuals around 1970 to roughly 550 today.

Field paleontology is a logistics and risk business, and the frontier is Antarctica

Lacovara's method: find sedimentary rocks of the right age (237 to 66 million years for non-avian dinosaurs), with exposure, and get as far from other paleontologists as possible. That last rule built his career. At Dreadnoughtus in southern Patagonia, he moved plaster-jacketed bones on horse-drawn sleds padded with prairie grass, rafted supplies across a glacial stream, and eventually drove a pickup through badlands where he could see only sky over the hood. He later hired a road scraper to cut a rough 15 km road. His closest call was climbing a 20–30 foot rock face in Montana or Wyoming with a 75-pound slab of pterosaur tracks on his back, no ropes, rock breaking away in his hands.

His mass estimate for Dreadnoughtus — 65 tons, about 13 African elephants or nine T. rex — rests on a tight correlation between body mass and the minimum shaft circumference of the humerus and femur in living quadrupeds. Bone histology showed disordered tissue near the edge, meaning the animal was still growing rapidly at death, at 65 tons. The skull and most of the neck were reconstructed by phylogenetic bracketing using Sarmientosaurus and Futalognosaurus; two neck vertebrae were all they had.

Other specifics worth filing away: Velociraptor was turkey-sized — "more of an opportunity than a problem" in your kitchen — and Jurassic Park used the name for a larger relative, likely Deinonychus. Quill insertion knobs are preserved on Velociraptor, so feathers are established for that group. Spinosaurus and Paralititan come from the Cretaceous North African mangrove ecosystem along the Tethys Seaway, which he would like to prospect in Libya and Algeria. The ultimate target is Antarctica: dinosaurs lived there at the pole in a boreal forest with half a year of darkness, an environment with no modern analog, and almost nothing is known about them.

He closes by giving Rogan two specimens from the Edelman extinction layer: a tooth from the crocodile Thoracosaurus and a tibia from a Cretaceous gharial-type crocodile, both 66 million years old and both killed by the impact.

For anyone allocating attention — or capital — across science-driven bets, the episode's unresolved tensions are the most instructive part. The soft-tissue and blood claims remain contested by the researchers best positioned to judge them. The Adams event is disputed. The consequences of a magnetic reversal are, by Lacovara's own admission, not well known. What holds is methodological rather than factual: falsifiability, prediction, and the willingness to let a hypothesis die. As he puts it, scientists rarely say "prove"; they say "we have failed to falsify." That standard is worth applying to every confident claim that crosses your feed — including the ones about asteroids, and the ones about whatever's coming next.
